articles.title: Tesla faces 'a few rough quarters' from end of US EV support: Musk
articles.content: STORY: Tesla's in for a few rough quarters , says its CEO Elon Musk, citing U.S. government cuts in support for electric vehicle makers.That's as Tesla posted its worst quarterly sales decline in over a decade Wednesday.Overall revenue fell 12%, despite the launch of a refreshed version of Tesla's best-selling Model Y SUV - which investors had hoped would boost sales.Revenue and profit were also hurt by a 51% dive in sales of regulatory credits.Those credits are bought from Tesla by other automakers who have difficulty complying with government emissions rules.The U.S. government later this year is cutting tax credits of up to $7,500 for EV buyers. :: FileWhen asked on a quarterly results conference call about the credits, Musk predicted a few rough quarters before a wave of revenue from self-driving software and services begins late next year.Tesla shares fell nearly 5% after his comments.In the meantime, Tesla says it is working on a new, cheaper car - with a few initial units made by the end of June.But production would ramp up next quarter, slower than initially expected.The company also said it continued to expect volume production of its custom-built robotaxi - called the Cybercab - and Semi Truck in 2026.Much of the company's trillion-dollar valuation hangs on its bet on humanoid robots and on its robotaxi service.But one analyst - CEO of Systematic Ventures Max Wolff - was skeptical of its chances to turn fortunes. The problem is there's other guys who have done more rides with less issues in a Robotaxi, particularly Waymo. This is sort of a major competitor here who's been at this longer, done many more rides and seems to have had a smoother integration. For the robotaxi business to rescue Tesla, as some had hoped, it would have had to have gotten a lot further, a lot faster than it has.

articles.title: The Week in Numbers: Japan gets a deal, Tesla takes a hit
articles.content: STORY: From Japan doing a deal on trade, to why Elon Musk says Tesla could hit a rough patch, this is the Week in Numbers.GRAPHIC 15%15% is the tariff set for Japanese goods by Donald Trump.“But I just signed the largest trade deal in history, I think maybe the largest deal in history with Japan.”The rate is less than threatened, and will cut the current duty on Japan’s key car exports.The news sent auto stocks surging in Tokyo, and one analyst said it could also mean the country can dodge a recession.GRAPHIC 12%12% was the plunge in sales for Tesla, marking its second straight quarterly drop.And boss Elon Musk said the firm could face a “few rough quarters”, not helped by Washington phasing out support for EVs.A cheaper new model could offer a boost, but production won’t ramp up for a while and investors aren’t happy, with Tesla shares plunging following the new figures.GRAPHIC $8.4 billion$8.4 billion is the value put on the merger between Paramount and Skydance, which has now got the green light from U.S. regulators.The deal had become politically charged, after Paramount paid millions to settle a lawsuit brought by Donald Trump over reporting by its CBS News unit.Critics including “Late Show” host Stephen Colbert have called the payment a “bribe” to secure the merger’s approval.GRAPHIC $50 billion$50 billion is how much AstraZeneca says it will invest in the U.S. by 2030.The drugs giant follows rivals in making a big pledge, as the industry scrambles to prepare for possible U.S. tariffs.For now it remains unclear when new duties might kick in, or at what level they will be set.GRAPHIC $1 billionAnd over $1 billion was the hit to profits for General Motors as a result of Trump’s tariffs.The auto giant says the trade turmoil could cost it $5 billion over the full year.Analysts say GM may need to cut investment plans to make up for the cost of the tariffs.
